newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel business seeks budget cuts, lower shekel.
newsitem.headline: Israel business seeks budget cuts, lower shekel.

text.p: The leaders of Israel's Manufacturers Association called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to prepare a comprehensive economic plan to tackle pressing issues.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday Dan Propper said the government must cut an additional one billion shekels from its budget in the coming year, lower interest rates, devalue the shekel and reduce the number of public sector employees.
The government has proposed a cut of 4.9 billion shekels or 3.2 percent (excluding debt servicing) from the 1997 budget.
Propper said the government also needed to encourage export-led growth and further liberalise the economy.

"The alternatives to this plan would be a Mexico-like crisis in Israel or a recession," he said, referring to last year's economic crisis in Mexico, which was sparked by a sharp devaluation of the peso.

If these steps are not feasible, the government should depreciate the shekel by lowering interest rates and allow annual inflation to reach 14 percent instead of the forecast 12 percent this year, Propper said.
"The rise in inflation is a price worth paying to avoid a recession or a Mexico-like crisis," Propper said.
He said the most pressing economic problems were the current account deficit in the balance of payments, the budget deficit and an overvalued shekel caused by the high interest rates.
"From 1993 to the first quarter of the year the shekel has appreciated 19 percent against the basket of foreign currencies (representing Israel's main trading partners)," he said.
Exports in 1996 will have zero growth against average growth of 11 to 15 percent in the preceding five years, he said.
Since the second half of 1995 industrial production has grown at a lower pace, rising 5.7 percent in the first half of 1996 compared with 8.7 percent in the first half of 1995.
The rate of investment in industry has also fallen significantly since last year, Propper said.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor told the government's coalition partners in the parliamentary finance committee on Monday that a 4.9 billion shekel cut in the 1997 budget was essential and the minimum required.

The government's budget proposal has met with opposition even from within its own coalition and critics say it will hit hardest at lower-income families. The budget proposal will be brought to parliament in October.
